Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Public Transport: Bus riding, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Arjun, a 27-year-old journalist, had always been passionate about storytelling. Growing up in a South Eastern Asian family in the United States, he had learned the value of resilience from an early age. His parents had faced their own adversities, and they instilled in him the belief that one could overcome any challenge with hard work and determination. But nothing could prepare him for the tumultuous relationship that would turn his world upside down.

It began innocently enough; Arjun met Sam through a mutual friend at a party. He was drawn to Sam’s charisma and charm, and they quickly fell into a whirlwind romance. However, in the months that followed, the relationship took a dark turn. What started as minor disagreements escalated into physical confrontations. Sam would lash out, often leaving Arjun feeling trapped and terrified. One night, after an argument that spiraled out of control, Sam physically assaulted him, leaving both emotional and physical scars that Arjun struggled to comprehend. 

In the aftermath, Arjun felt a profound sense of confusion and shame. He found himself replaying the event over and over, feeling as if it were happening again each time he closed his eyes. The memory consumed him; he could feel the pain in his body as if it were present in that moment, every bruise and ache coming back to life with vivid clarity. “You should have known better,” he would tell himself, spiraling into a cycle of self-blame and rumination that haunted his waking hours. The more he dwelled on what had happened, the more inadequate he felt, convinced that he should have prevented the violence. 

Arjun’s ability to trust others began to erode, and he found it impossible to believe that anyone could keep him safe. Even when his friends and family reassured him that he was no longer in danger, he dismissed their words. It was as if a shadow loomed over him, a constant reminder that harm could come from anywhere, at any time. He began to notice that his anxiety heightened when he encountered situations that reminded him of his trauma. Public transport, once a mundane part of his daily life, became a source of dread. The sound of the bus doors closing felt ominous, and the presence of men nearby sent him spiraling into panic. He would often ride with his heart racing, convinced that the men around him were potential threats. 

In his efforts to cope, Arjun developed maladaptive strategies that further entrenched his feelings of inadequacy. He started to suppress his anger, believing that expressing it would only lead to more harm. Instead, he internalized those feelings, convincing himself that he had no right to be angry about what had happened to him. This suppression extended to his basic needs; he began undereating, using food restriction as a misguided method of coping. The hunger pangs became a physical manifestation of his emotional pain, and he felt a sense of control in denying himself nourishment, even as it left him feeling weak and fatigued.

Arjun’s nights were plagued by alertness; he often woke in the middle of the night, convinced that he needed to check if he was safe. The fear had taken root so deeply that he struggled to find solace even in the comfort of his own home. His relationship with his partner began to suffer as well; he would withdraw emotionally, fearing closeness and intimacy. He felt that he was dragging Sam into the darkness he couldn't escape, and he couldn't bear the thought of putting anyone else at risk.

As the months dragged on, Arjun’s mental state deteriorated. He was consumed by thoughts of harm and mistrust, leading to a pervasive sense of isolation. It was during a particularly anxious moment on a crowded bus, when he felt the walls closing in and the memories flooding back, that he realized he could no longer manage alone. He had come to believe that seeking help was a sign of weakness, but he was exhausted from the fight against his own mind. 

Finally, after weeks of turmoil, Arjun found himself sitting in a therapist’s office, his heart racing as he recounted the trauma. What frightened him most was the fear that he would always feel this way, trapped in a cycle of pain and distrust. Yet, deep down, he hoped for relief — for a way to reclaim his life and trust in the safety of the world around him once more.
